course.title: AP Precalculus
course.description: Build the function toolkit that calculus depends on: how quantities change together, polynomial and rational functions, exponential and logarithmic models, and trigonometric and polar functions.
course.previewDescription: Study how outputs change with inputs, then use polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions to describe patterns and build models.

unit.title: Polynomial and Rational Functions
unit.description: See how outputs change with inputs, then use rates of change, zeros, end behavior, asymptotes, and holes to describe polynomial and rational functions and build models from them.

topic.title: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change
topic.summary: Degree, leading term, and leading coefficient, relative and absolute extrema, extrema between real zeros, and points of inflection.

lesson.title: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change
lesson.summary: Degree, leading term, and leading coefficient, relative and absolute extrema, extrema between real zeros, and points of inflection.
learningGoals: 1.4.A Identify key characteristics of polynomial functions related to rates of change.
lesson.bigIdea: Where the rate of change of a polynomial function changes sign, the function has a relative maximum or minimum. Where the rate of change changes from increasing to decreasing, or the reverse, the graph has a point of inflection.
lesson.context: Topics 1.1 to 1.3 described output values and rates of change in general. Polynomial functions are the first family where those ideas combine into several turning points and changes in concavity on one graph.

sections.title: 1.4.A · A polynomial function has a degree, a leading term, and a leading coefficient.

blocks.text: A nonconstant polynomial function of x is any function representation equivalent to p(x) = aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₂x² + a₁x + a₀, where n is a positive integer, each aᵢ is a real number, and aₙ is nonzero. The polynomial has degree n, the leading term is aₙxⁿ, and the leading coefficient is aₙ.

blocks.caption: Degree, leading term, and leading coefficient

blocks.text: A product such as x(x − 1)(x + 2) is a polynomial because it is equivalent to x³ + x² − 2x. Expressions such as 5/x or √x are not polynomials, because they are not equivalent to a sum of terms with positive integer powers of x.

sections.takeaway: Write the terms from highest to lowest power: the first term is the leading term, and its power is the degree.

sections.title: 1.4.A · Relative extrema occur where a polynomial switches between increasing and decreasing.

blocks.text: Where a polynomial function switches between increasing and decreasing, or at an included endpoint of a polynomial with a restricted domain, the function has a local, or relative, maximum or minimum output value. If a relative maximum is greater than all other output values, it is a global, or absolute, maximum. If a relative minimum is less than all other output values, it is a global, or absolute, minimum.

As x increases from −2 to −1, f(x) increases from −2 to 2, and from −1 to 1, f(x) decreases to −2. So f has a relative maximum of 2 at x = −1 and a relative minimum of −2 at x = 1. Neither is absolute, because a cubic's output values increase without bound in one direction and decrease without bound in the other.

A polynomial function of even degree has either a global maximum or a global minimum. For a quadratic function, the global maximum or global minimum occurs at the vertex. Both ends of the graph of an even-degree polynomial point the same way, which is why one of them must exist.

blocks.title: Write it like the AP Exam
blocks.text: f has a relative maximum at x = −1 because f changes from increasing to decreasing at x = −1. The relative maximum value is f(−1) = 2.

blocks.caption: Graph of f(x) = x³ − 3x, with a relative maximum at x = −1 and a relative minimum at x = 1
blocks.alt: A cubic curve that rises to a peak at (−1, 2), falls to a low point at (1, −2), then rises again.

sections.takeaway: A relative extremum is greatest or least nearby. An absolute extremum is greatest or least over the whole domain.

sections.title: 1.4.A · Between two distinct real zeros there is a relative extremum.

blocks.text: Between every two distinct real zeros of a nonconstant polynomial function, there must be at least one input value corresponding to a relative maximum or relative minimum. The output values leave 0 and return to 0, so the function must change direction in between.

For g(x) = x³ − 4x = x(x − 2)(x + 2), with zeros at −2, 0, and 2, technology shows a relative maximum of about 3.079 at x ≈ −1.155 between −2 and 0, and a relative minimum of about −3.079 at x ≈ 1.155 between 0 and 2.

sections.takeaway: Two distinct real zeros guarantee at least one relative extremum between them, not exactly one.

sections.title: 1.4.A · Points of inflection occur where the rate of change changes from increasing to decreasing, or the reverse.

blocks.text: Points of inflection of a polynomial function occur at input values where the rate of change of the function changes from increasing to decreasing or from decreasing to increasing. This is where the graph changes from concave up to concave down or from concave down to concave up.

blocks.caption: Changes in f(x) = x³ over intervals of length 1

blocks.title: Write it like the AP Exam
blocks.text: The graph of f has a point of inflection at x = 0 because the rate of change of f changes from decreasing to increasing there, so the graph changes from concave down to concave up.

sections.takeaway: An extremum is a change in direction. A point of inflection is a change in concavity.

connections.title: Quadratic functions are the simplest case
connections.body: A quadratic function has one vertex, which is its absolute extremum, and no point of inflection, because its average rates of change change at a constant rate in one direction.
connections.transferQuestion: Why can the graph of a quadratic function never have a point of inflection?
connections.feedback: Its rate of change is always increasing or always decreasing, so its concavity never changes.

connections.title: Zeros and end behavior complete the picture
connections.body: Topic 1.5 links real zeros to linear factors and to how the graph meets the x-axis, and Topic 1.6 uses the leading term to describe end behavior.
connections.transferQuestion: What would you want to know about a polynomial before sketching its graph?
connections.feedback: Its real zeros and their multiplicities, its end behavior, and then its extrema and concavity.

glossary.definition: The graph of a function is concave up on intervals in which the rate of change is increasing.
The graph of a function is concave down on intervals in which the rate of change is decreasing.
